8	Degeneracy matters here: one can merge the two middle critical points of the usual height function on \(S^2\times S^2\) into a single, highly degenerate critical point. A sufficiently small autonomous Hamiltonian obtained this way has exactly three fixed points.

10	## 1. Lower bound
11	
12	We use the **degenerate Arnold cup-length theorem**: on a closed rational weakly monotone symplectic manifold, a Hamiltonian diffeomorphism with finitely many fixed points has at least
13	\[
14	1+\operatorname{cuplength}(M;\mathbb Q)
15	\]
16	distinct contractible fixed points.
17	
18	Its hypotheses hold here. If \(A=[S^2\times\{\mathrm{pt}\}]\) and \(B=[\{\mathrm{pt}\}\times S^2]\), then
19	\[
20	\omega(A)=\omega(B)=4\pi,\qquad
21	c_1(TM)(A)=c_1(TM)(B)=2.
22	\]
23	Thus \([\omega]=2\pi c_1(TM)\); in particular \(M\) is rational and positive monotone. Also \(M\) is simply connected, so all the relevant periodic orbits are contractible.
24	
25	The cohomology ring is
26	\[
27	H^*(M;\mathbb Q)=\mathbb Q[\alpha,\beta]/(\alpha^2,\beta^2),
28	\qquad |\alpha|=|\beta|=2,
29	\]
30	and \(\alpha\beta\ne0\). Its cup-length is two. Consequently,
31	\[
32	\#\operatorname{Fix}(\varphi_H^1)\ge3.
33	\]
34	
35	We now construct an example attaining this bound. This is the part where allowing degenerate fixed points is essential.
36	
37	## 2. An explicit function with three critical points
38	
39	Start with
40	\[
41	f(x,y)=x_3+y_3.
42	\]
43	It has four critical points: a minimum, a maximum, and the two index-two saddles
44	\[
45	(N,S),\qquad(S,N),
46	\]
47	both at value zero. We will replace a ball containing precisely those two saddles by a function with one critical point.
48	
49	### 2.1 Coordinates around an arc joining the saddles
50	
51	Put
52	\[
53	\begin{aligned}
54	q&=(\cos t\sin s,\ \sin t,\ \cos t\cos s),\\
55	e_1&=(\cos s,\ 0,\ -\sin s),\\
56	e_2&=(-\sin t\sin s,\ \cos t,\ -\sin t\cos s).
57	\end{aligned}
58	\]
59	These form an orthonormal frame. For small \(a,b,t\), set
60	\[
61	p=ae_1+be_2,\qquad
62	x=\sqrt{1-a^2-b^2}\,q+p,\qquad
63	y=-\sqrt{1-a^2-b^2}\,q+p.
64	\]
65	Then \(|x|=|y|=1\). These are smooth coordinates near the arc
66	\[
67	0\le s\le\pi,\qquad t=a=b=0,
68	\]
69	whose endpoints are the two saddles. Injectivity follows from
70	\[
71	q=\frac{x-y}{|x-y|},\qquad p=\frac{x+y}{2}.
72	\]
73	
74	In these coordinates,
75	\[
76	f=-2\bigl(a\sin s+b\sin t\cos s\bigr).                 \tag{1}
77	\]
78	
79	Choose \(0<\delta<\pi/4\), and write
80	\[
81	A=\frac\pi2+\delta,\qquad u=s-\frac\pi2.
82	\]
83	The ellipsoid
84	\[
85	B=\left\{
86	\frac{u^2}{A^2}+\frac{t^2+a^2+b^2}{\delta^2}\le1
87	\right\}                                                   \tag{2}
88	\]
89	is a smoothly embedded closed four-ball. It contains exactly the two saddle critical points of \(f\).
90	
91	### 2.2 A boundary adapted to \(f\)
92	
93	Define the smooth vector field
94	\[
95	\begin{aligned}
96	Y_s&=\tfrac12\sin s\cos s,\\
97	Y_t&=\tfrac12t,\\
98	Y_a&=\left(1-\tfrac12\cos^2s\right)a,\\
99	Y_b&=\left(1+\tfrac12\sin^2s-\tfrac12t\cot t\right)b,
100	\end{aligned}                                               \tag{3}
101	\]
102	where \(t\cot t\) is assigned its smooth value \(1\) at zero.
103	
104	Direct differentiation of (1) gives the important identity
105	\[
106	Yf=f.                                                       \tag{4}
107	\]
108	
109	Moreover, \(Y\) points strictly outward along \(\partial B\). Here are details of that assertion. Let
110	\[
111	R^2=t^2+a^2+b^2,\qquad
112	P=\frac{u^2}{A^2}+\frac{R^2}{\delta^2}.
113	\]
114	Since \(t\cot t\le1\) for \(|t|<\pi/4\),
115	\[
116	YR^2-R^2
117	=a^2\sin^2s+b^2(1+\sin^2s-t\cot t)\ge0.
118	\]
119	Hence, on \(P=1\),
120	\[
121	YP\ge
122	\frac{A^2-u^2+u\sin s\cos s}{A^2}>0.                         \tag{5}
123	\]
124	For completeness, put \(v=|u|\). When \(v\le\pi/2\),
125	\[
126	u\sin s\cos s=-v\sin v\cos v,\qquad
127	v\sin v\cos v\le v(\pi/2-v),
128	\]
129	so the numerator in (5) is at least \(A^2-\pi^2/4>0\).
130	When \(\pi/2\le v\le A<\pi\), its last term is nonnegative; it is strictly positive if \(v=A\).
131	
132	Let \(g=f|_{\partial B}\). Zero is a regular value of \(g\). Indeed, if \(g=0\) and \(dg=0\) at a boundary point, then \(df\) vanishes on \(T\partial B\) and, by (4), on the transverse vector \(Y\). This would make that boundary point a critical point of \(f\), which it is not.
133	
134	### 2.3 Replace the interior by a flat cone
135	
136	The flow of \(Y\) supplies a collar of \(\partial B\), with radial coordinate \(r\) near \(1\), in which (4) becomes
137	\[
138	f(r,\theta)=r\,g(\theta).
139	\]
140	By the collar theorem, choose a parametrization of \(B\) by the unit four-ball agreeing with these collar coordinates.
141	
142	Choose a smooth nonincreasing function \(\chi:[0,1]\to[0,1]\) which equals \(1\) near zero and \(0\) near one. Set
143	\[
144	\rho(r)=r\exp\!\left(-\frac{\chi(r)}{r^2}\right)\quad(r>0),
145	\qquad \rho(0)=0.
146	\]
147	This function is flat at zero, equals \(r\) near one, and
148	\[
149	\frac{\rho'(r)}{\rho(r)}
150	=\frac1r-\frac{\chi'(r)}{r^2}+\frac{2\chi(r)}{r^3}>0.
151	\]
152	
153	Replace \(f\) inside \(B\) by
154	\[
155	F(r,\theta)=\rho(r)g(\theta),\qquad F(0)=0,
156	\]
157	and leave it unchanged outside \(B\). It matches smoothly near \(\partial B\), and flatness makes it smooth at the center.
158	
159	For \(r>0\),
160	\[
161	dF=\rho'(r)g(\theta)\,dr+\rho(r)\,dg(\theta).
162	\]
163	If this vanished, we would have \(g=0\) and \(dg=0\), contradicting the regular-value property. Thus the center is the only critical point in \(B\).
164	
165	The resulting smooth \(F:M\to\mathbb R\) therefore has precisely **three** critical points: the original minimum, the original maximum, and the new flat critical point.
166	
167	## 3. Turn the function into a Hamiltonian with exactly three fixed points
168	
169	Take the time-independent Hamiltonian
170	\[
171	H_t=\varepsilon F
172	\]
173	for sufficiently small \(\varepsilon>0\). We must exclude nonconstant one-periodic trajectories—not merely count equilibria.
174	
175	Embed \(M\subset\mathbb R^6\), and extend \(X_F\) to a smooth compactly supported vector field \(Z\) on \(\mathbb R^6\). Let \(L\) be a global Lipschitz constant for \(Z\).
176	
177	Suppose \(x(t)\) is a nonconstant one-periodic solution of
178	\[
179	\dot x=\varepsilon Z(x).
180	\]
181	Write \(\bar x=\int_0^1x(t)\,dt\), and set
182	\[
183	E=\int_0^1|\dot x|^2\,dt,\qquad
184	V=\int_0^1|x-\bar x|^2\,dt.
185	\]
186	Periodicity and the Lipschitz estimate give
187	\[
188	\begin{aligned}
189	E
190	&=\varepsilon\int_0^1
191	 \langle\dot x,Z(x)-Z(\bar x)\rangle\,dt\\
192	&\le\varepsilon L\sqrt{EV}.
193	\end{aligned}
194	\]
195	The periodic Wirtinger inequality says \(V\le E/(4\pi^2)\). Since \(E>0\), this implies
196	\[
197	1\le\frac{\varepsilon L}{2\pi}.
198	\]
199	Choosing \(\varepsilon L<2\pi\) excludes all such trajectories.
200	
201	Thus the time-one fixed points are exactly the equilibria:
202	\[
203	\operatorname{Fix}(\varphi_{\varepsilon F}^1)
204	=\operatorname{Crit}(F),
205	\]
206	and there are exactly three.
207
